scenario: AITA for giving my girlfriend pointers on how to cook better? | So my girlfriend is pissed at me and has a cooking "strike" because, and I quote,"if you are so much better than me at cooking you can do it yourself". We moved in together 6 months ago (been together for 2 before it) and we came to an agreement that she will do the cooking since she comes 2h earlier from work and I was all on board for having a hot meal ready when I come home. The thing is she is not exactly good at it. She isnt terrible, everything she makes is edible but is far off from the standard I was used to. So, I started to give her pointers. After all she cant get better if she doesnt know that something is off. The thing is that she "snapped" when my mother came to visit and I casually said that she could give my girlfriend some cooking advice. My girlfriend nodded and smiled and generally seemed fine in the moment but as soon as the doors closed behind my mother my girlfriend went ballistic, accused me of humiliating her and her cooking in front of my family and stormed off. Since then I apologised saying that I am sorry for giving her constructive criticism in front of my mom but it didnt calm her much and she still refuses to make anything food-related at home for me. I think she is overreacting, I never complained about her cooking or throw it out. I was just being helpful. I miss her cooking, not gonna lie, so I might as well ask here if I stepped over the line somewhere. AITA or is my girlfriend crazy?

prediction.raw: I would say: 1 (You are the asshole). While your intention might have been to help your girlfriend improve her cooking, the way you approached the situation was likely perceived as condescending and critical. By constantly pointing out what she was doing wrong, you may have made her feel belittled and unappreciated. The fact that you did this in front of your mother, someone she might feel intimidated by or want to impress, made the situation even more embarrassing and humiliating for her. It's not just about the cooking itself, but about the way you communicated your feedback. Instead of offering constructive criticism in a gentle and supportive manner, you came across as a culinary expert who was correcting her mistakes. This can be perceived as patronizing and dismissive of her efforts. Additionally, the fact that you didn't seem to consider her feelings or perspective, and instead focused on your own preferences and expectations, suggests that you might not have been as empathetic or understanding as you could have been. It's not about being "right" or "wrong" in terms of cooking techniques, but about respecting your partner's feelings and boundaries. By apologizing for giving constructive criticism in front of your mom, you acknowledged that you might have overstepped, but it's clear that the issue runs deeper than just that one incident. To resolve this, you might want to have an open and honest conversation with your girlfriend, listening to her perspective and feelings, and working together to find a more supportive and collaborative approach to cooking and feedback.
